title: Mission over Model: What Might AI Mean for an Organization Like Carnegie?
gist: Carnegie's interim president Dan Baer argues that because AI has democratized content creation, think tanks should publish fewer but more genuinely novel pieces, shifting scholars from information producers to 'sherpas' who guide audiences through information surplus via convening, fieldwork, and charismatic public communication. He goes further, floating the provocation that Carnegie may need to withhold research from public/LLM distribution and build proprietary data sets, because model-mediated answers strip attribution and the credentialing effect that funders and policymakers respond to.

themes.theme: Content surplus inverts the think-tank model

insights.claim: Think tanks were built for a world of research-content scarcity, and that founding premise — unmet demand for high-quality written analysis on specialized topics — no longer holds once AI makes content creation nearly free.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: The scarcity rent that funded policy research, trade publishing, and analyst content is gone; business models built on producing explainers are structurally impaired.
insights.quote: If the internet democratized the distribution of content, AI has democratized the creation of content.
insights.locator: If the internet democratized the distribution

insights.claim: The internet democratized distribution of content while AI has democratized its creation, and the combination — not either alone — is what changes the competitive backdrop for knowledge organizations.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Two-stage disruption framing: distribution incumbents were disrupted in round one, production incumbents in round two.
insights.quote: The combination of these two phenomena has changed the backdrop against which we work.
insights.locator: If the internet democratized the distribution

insights.claim: Carnegie's institutional mark of quality historically meant 'unbiased, rigorous, and fact-based,' but in an AI world that signal is no longer differentiating and must be replaced by a claim to novelty.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Brand equity built on accuracy and rigor commoditizes when models supply both cheaply; the durable brand asset becomes originality.
insights.quote: This information and analysis is new, novel, and different from what other sources, including LLMs, provide.
insights.locator: For decades, Carnegie’s name has been a mark

insights.claim: The demand side has flipped from information scarcity to information saturation, so the value of an analyst shifts from adding to the pile to helping decisionmakers sort it.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Curation and filtering — not production volume — is where pricing power moves in any information business.
insights.quote: The consumers of our content used to be thirsty for knowledge; now they are swimming in it.
insights.locator: Genuinely novel research will be distinctly helpful

insights.claim: Distribution of policy research was once a physical, high-friction act — printing reports, dropping them at Senate office buildings, mailing them to the Pentagon — and that friction was itself the moat.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Historical baseline for how much of institutional influence was logistics rather than insight; zero-friction distribution erases that advantage.
insights.quote: We printed copies of these reports and dropped them off at Senate office buildings or mailed them to the Pentagon knowing that policymakers would eagerly consume them.
insights.locator: There was a time when Carnegie could produce a report

themes.theme: Fewer publications, not more — against the productivity narrative

insights.claim: External funders are already beginning to expect research organizations to demonstrate AI-driven productivity gains, pressuring them to show more output per dollar.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Funder and investor expectations of AI productivity dividends are becoming an explicit contractual pressure in knowledge sectors — watch for the same in consulting, law, and media budgets.
insights.quote: My colleagues and I have already seen early signs that external funders of our work will increasingly expect us to demonstrate productivity gains by incorporating AI into our research process.
insights.locator: 1) We might produce less, not more.

insights.claim: The consensus AI productivity expectation is wrong for research organizations: the correct response to cheap content is to publish fewer pieces, not more, while still doing the job right.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Direct challenge to the 'AI raises output' thesis in knowledge work — measured output volume may be a misleading KPI for AI adoption.
insights.quote: My intuition is that this expectation is incorrect, and that in the coming years, we may produce fewer publications, not more (and still be doing our job right).
insights.locator: My intuition is that this expectation is incorrect

insights.claim: The pre-AI research pyramid had a thin top slice of genuinely novel work, a broader middle of synthesizing research, and a broad base of expository commentary; the bottom two layers are the ones AI collapses.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: A clean segmentation tool for judging which knowledge-work outputs (and which staff) are exposed to model substitution.
insights.quote: In the coming years, I expect the bottom two layers of the pyramid will significantly decrease in size, and the top slice will become the primary focus of research effort.
insights.locator: If one imagines a pyramid of the research content

insights.claim: Explainers, primers, and issue overviews are the research outputs most obviously accelerated or replaced by AI, and they will no longer differentiate researchers.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Media and research franchises whose economics rest on explainer content face direct model substitution.
insights.quote: These kinds of explainers and overviews are not likely to be how we distinguish ourselves as researchers going forward
insights.locator: These kinds of explainers and overviews

insights.claim: Surviving research output should concentrate on three things: directly challenging prevailing assessments, leveraging primary research and fieldwork, and compressing large information sets into heuristics and frameworks.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: A practical filter for what analysis still commands attention and budget when baseline synthesis is free.
insights.quote: directly challenges prevailing assessments or conventional wisdom, leverages primary research and fieldwork, and crystallizes or reframes large amounts of information into heuristics or frameworks
insights.locator: My hypothesis is that we should focus more

insights.claim: The reason to abandon synthesizing and expository research is not brand differentiation but impact: those product types have no clear route to influencing decisions in a content-surplus world.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI threat as a demand-side impact problem rather than a supply-side competition problem.
insights.quote: the other types of research product have a less obvious route to impact in a changed world
insights.locator: Importantly, this focus on “genuinely novel”

insights.claim: Producing genuinely novel conclusions takes longer than summarizing known material, so time spent writing may rise even as published word count falls.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Cost per published unit of genuinely original knowledge work may increase under AI, inverting naive unit-economics models.
insights.quote: we may spend more time in the old-fashioned writing process than we do now and produce fewer published words
insights.locator: A corollary hypothesis to my first intuition

themes.theme: Skill shift: curation, dialectic, and convening

insights.claim: The core distinguishing skills of a researcher shift toward curation, refinement, and creative improvement of ideas, usually in collaboration rather than solo authorship.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Hiring and evaluation criteria in knowledge organizations move away from writing craft toward idea selection and synthesis judgment.
insights.quote: our core skills will be curation, refinement, and creative improvement of ideas, often in collaboration with others
insights.locator: 2) As researchers, our core skills

insights.claim: Careers built on being a clever, astute writer rather than an innovative thinker were viable only because ideas needed human artisans to render them into prose — the same way portraiture was needed before photography.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Precise identification of the exposed labor segment: the translation layer between idea and prose, not idea generation itself.
insights.quote: ideas needed human artisans to translate them into prose
insights.locator: The scholars who got by because they were good writers

insights.claim: As models absorb summarization of context, the human researcher's job moves from explaining how an institution like NATO protects European security to reimagining what European security should be.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Concrete template for where human value migrates within any analytical workflow: from description to redesign.
insights.quote: the human scholar (who used to spend time laying out historical context and approach) will need to focus more on what reimagining European security might look like
insights.locator: When AI can summarize the history and intricacies

insights.claim: Writing has always produced two outputs — the publication and the expert — so outsourcing drafting to AI risks destroying the training mechanism that creates expertise in the first place.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: A second-order risk in AI adoption: near-term efficiency gains can erode the talent pipeline that supplies future judgment.
insights.quote: the process of writing also produces the expert
insights.locator: The kind of writing that we do has always had two products

insights.claim: AI used as a sounding board will not substitute for human-to-human intellectual exchange, which becomes more essential to research as automated synthesis spreads.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Supports demand for in-person, high-trust formats even as digital content deflates in value.
insights.quote: I suspect that these exchanges will not replace the value of human-to-human exchange, and that the latter will actually be even more essential to the research process in the years ahead
insights.locator: While many scholars are already learning to use AI

insights.claim: Convening will shift from being a dissemination channel to being a primary mechanism of knowledge creation, making small workshop-format gatherings more valuable than lectures and speaker panels.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Bullish signal for high-touch, curated event businesses and closed-door networks; bearish for broadcast-style conference formats.
insights.quote: I suspect we will see convening as progressively more essential to knowledge creation, rather than to dissemination.
insights.locator: And I suspect we will see convening

insights.claim: The ability to attract high-quality participants with diverse views — not the ability to publish — will mark out the leaders of epistemic communities.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Convening power becomes a measurable institutional asset; organizations without a convening strategy will be forced to build one.
insights.quote: Being able to attract high-quality participants with a diversity of views will distinguish institutions and individual researchers as leaders of epistemic communities.
insights.locator: Being able to attract high-quality participants

themes.theme: The expertise premium and the charismatic intellectual

insights.claim: Carnegie exists to correct a market failure — the market and bureaucracy will not supply decisionmakers with the information they need for peace-promoting choices — and that failure does not disappear when content becomes abundant.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Frames nonprofit research as a persistent market-failure play, meaning abundance changes the product but not the underlying demand.
insights.quote: Carnegie exists to compensate for a market failure
insights.locator: 3) In our post-expert world

insights.claim: Research staff move from being information producers to information guides, mediating the intersection between information and structures of power in politics, media, the private sector, and culture.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: The 'guide' role is the defensible position in an abundance economy — applies equally to sell-side research, media, and advisory businesses.
insights.quote: Where Carnegie’s research staff were once almost entirely information producers, we will increasingly function as information guides helping audiences navigate information surplus.
insights.locator: Where Carnegie’s research staff were once

insights.claim: Public obsession with AI hallucinations has functioned as collective self-soothing about the supremacy of human-produced content, distracting from the fact that models already produce moderately sophisticated primers well enough for most use cases.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Contrarian read on the safest-sounding bear case for AI in knowledge work; the substitution risk is already realized in the majority of use cases.
insights.quote: the focus on hallucinations, while reasonable and important, has been a mechanism for collective self-soothing about the enduring supremacy of human-produced content
insights.locator: There has been a persistent public scrutiny of AI hallucinations

insights.claim: Hallucinations will not be eliminated in the near term but will become more subtle as models improve, making errors harder rather than easier to catch.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Verification tooling and human review demand rises rather than falls as model quality improves — subtle error is costlier to detect.
insights.quote: hallucinations may not be eliminated in the near term, but they will become more subtle
insights.locator: The models will get better

insights.claim: AI has effectively given the world access to infinite encyclopedia articles, which is enough for schoolwork-grade needs but structurally insufficient for nuanced judgment.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: A calibration heuristic for where models saturate demand and where human analysis retains a bid.
insights.quote: AI means that the world has access to literally infinite encyclopedia articles.
insights.locator: When I was growing up, we had a thirty-volume encyclopedia

insights.claim: Decisionmakers with economic and political exposure will demand assurance both that model output passed human expert review and that it was not distorted by the national, commercial, or political biases of the model's owners.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Points to a market for independent human verification and model-bias attestation aimed at high-stakes decisionmakers.
insights.quote: they will want to know that it hasn’t been distorted by the national, commercial, or political biases of the models’ owners or creators
insights.locator: They will want to know that the content generated

insights.claim: Senate staffers and analysts at major investment banks now form views partly from social media video and graphs relatives saw on X, not just industry publications and name-brand newspapers.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Elite decision inputs have retail-ized; information campaigns aimed at mass channels now propagate into institutional decisions.
insights.quote: Senate staffers and analysts at major investment banks don’t just read industry publications and name-brand newspapers
insights.locator: Senate staffers and analysts at major investment banks

insights.claim: In an environment of generated authoritative-seeming content, facts no longer speak for themselves and require credentialed experts to speak for them and elevate rigorous ideas.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Trust intermediation becomes the scarce good; reputation-heavy institutions gain relative value versus commodity content.
insights.quote: we are in an era when facts do not, in fact, speak for themselves
insights.locator: Audiences (and experts themselves) will increasingly learn

insights.claim: Every significant research product will need a suite of derivative marketing artifacts — an op-ed version plus short-form video and media appearances — because publication alone no longer reaches audiences.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Distribution and repackaging costs become a permanent line item in knowledge production budgets, favoring organizations with media capability.
insights.quote: Every piece of research we do may require a suite of derivative products that essentially function as marketing materials for the core insights.
insights.locator: Every piece of research we do may require

insights.claim: Op-eds still reach policy elites but are decreasingly effective at shaping the political context in which elites deliberate, so non-op-ed formats matter more for moving the Overton window.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Influence strategies must target the mass information environment upstream of elite deliberation, not just elite channels.
insights.quote: they are less and less effective at shaping the political context in which policy elites deliberate
insights.locator: And while op-ed–style pieces are likely to remain

insights.claim: The successful expert profile shifts toward 'charismatic intellectuals' rather than bookish solitary scholars, a skill set research institutions have not historically hired or trained for.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Talent scarcity and repricing in knowledge organizations: communication-forward experts get a wage premium while pure research profiles do not.
insights.quote: We haven’t historically prioritized this skill set when hiring
insights.locator: My hunch is that as a consequence of this reality

insights.claim: As AI-generated content regresses toward a synthetic mean in tone and tenor, the distinctiveness of a human mind at work becomes an attention asset that competes favorably.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Stylistic distinctiveness becomes economically valuable as machine output homogenizes — a scarcity-of-voice trade.
insights.quote: the aesthetic attraction of a beautiful human mind at work and its distinctive way of communicating ideas may compete favorably for attention
insights.locator: As AI-generated content proliferates

themes.theme: AI as a capability unlock, not a replacement

insights.claim: The dominant framing error is worrying about how AI replicates existing work rather than asking what previously impossible work it enables.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Reframes AI ROI assessment from cost substitution to capability expansion — the higher-value and less-measured half.
insights.quote: we should spend more time thinking about how the existence of the models might prompt us to do things we don’t
insights.locator: 4) We have focused too much on how AI might replicate

insights.claim: Social-science-trained researchers over-index on AI's effect on writing because writing is their native craft, and so under-invest in AI-enabled quantitative methods.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Professional training background predicts which AI use cases an organization sees and which it misses — a diagnostic for adoption blind spots.
insights.quote: The bias to be more concerned about AI and writing reflects our typical background
insights.locator: The bias to be more concerned about AI and writing

insights.claim: AI has democratized the 'beyond Excel' frontier, putting analysis that recently required advanced programmers or large data-analytics teams within reach of a single researcher.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Direct threat to the billable value of junior quantitative headcount and specialist data teams across research and finance.
insights.quote: AI has democratized the “beyond Excel” frontier
insights.locator: First, AI has democratized

insights.claim: Datasets that were theoretically possible but economically unfeasible are now buildable — for example, a coded, searchable, translated archive of all EU foreign ministry statements from 1998 to 2024 across 200 key terms.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: The cost curve of proprietary dataset construction has collapsed, making bespoke data a newly viable moat for small research shops.
insights.quote: a historical archive of the statements of all EU countries’ foreign ministries from 1998 to 2024, coded and searchable by any one of 200 key terms, translated into English
insights.locator: Using AI to scrape data from the internet

insights.claim: AI makes it practical to marry previously separate datasets, such as combining World Bank macroeconomic data, IPCC climate data, and Transparency International corruption data across the fifty largest economies.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Cross-domain data fusion becomes cheap, opening novel macro and country-risk signals to non-specialist teams.
insights.quote: organizing World Bank macroeconomic data, Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change data, and Transparency International corruption data by country for the fifty largest economies in the world
insights.locator: And it allows us to marry two or more existing data sets

insights.claim: Vibe coding and cheap compute let policy researchers run Monte Carlo simulations to complement qualitative war games, including on escalation toward nuclear conflict.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Quantitative probabilistic methods migrating into geopolitical risk analysis — expect more model-backed escalation estimates informing policy and markets.
insights.quote: Policy researchers might increasingly use such analyses to complement more qualitative observations drawn from, say, war game simulations of escalation toward nuclear conflict.
insights.locator: Third, the computing power and vibe coding capabilities

insights.claim: Because expanded data capability is available to every competitor, the durable comparative advantage stays with fieldwork and closed-door relationships of trust that generate insights people will not put in writing.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Identifies the non-replicable input in an AI-commoditized analysis stack: privately sourced human intelligence.
insights.quote: Curating closed-door spaces and relationships of trust so that people share reflections and insights in person that they wouldn’t share in written communication will remain essential.
insights.locator: Of course, other researchers will have access

insights.claim: Large-scale data analysis changes the economics of research by allowing hypotheses once testable only with anecdote to be empirically validated — and, crucially, allowing bad hunches to be rejected faster.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Faster falsification lowers the cost of being wrong, which raises the optimal rate of hypothesis generation in any research shop.
insights.quote: reject hunches more quickly in which we might have previously invested precious time in vain
insights.locator: We can answer questions with moderate confidence

insights.claim: A shift to data-driven research is a methodological change affecting every stage from question framing to fact-checking, and requires significant retraining and upskilling of existing research staff.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: The real AI cost for knowledge organizations is workforce retraining, not tooling — budget and timeline implications are underestimated.
insights.quote: It is not a matter of adding a few extra graphs to a research paper—it’s a methodological shift that would affect all stages of the research process
insights.locator: A vast expansion of data-driven and quantitative research

themes.theme: Open access under pressure: the proprietary-knowledge bet

insights.claim: A leading nonprofit research institution is openly considering abandoning its default of free public research and keeping more of its product private — framed as the author's most provocative intuition.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: If open-access research institutions begin walling off output, the free public knowledge supply that trains and grounds models starts to shrink.
insights.quote: I wonder if we will consider modifying that approach and keeping more of our research product private
insights.locator: 5) We will wrestle with the question

insights.claim: Distribution through LLMs deepens reach beyond a small elite audience and can make an institution's research part of the basis for general societal understanding.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: The upside case for feeding models: epistemic share of voice at scale, which may outweigh lost attribution for some publishers.
insights.quote: If the models become primary widespread sources of human understanding, our research transmitted through them could shape epistemic communities and general understanding.
insights.locator: In its first years, commercially available AI

insights.claim: Model summarization destroys the curation and contextualization layer, so a repackaged executive summary untraceable to its foundational research fails the publisher's actual objective.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Core of the publisher-versus-model dispute stated in impact terms rather than copyright terms — a different basis for withholding content.
insights.quote: a repackaged executive summary that isn’t traceable to the foundational research is not achieving our objectives
insights.locator: If our value-add is providing deep research

insights.claim: Research products that stand alone with a byline carry a credentialing effect that model-mediated answers do not: a Claude query is far less likely to produce a congressional hearing invitation or a call from a foreign ministry than a well-written report or op-ed.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Attribution loss through AI intermediation destroys the downstream commercial and influence funnel, not just traffic — the strongest argument for content withholding.
insights.quote: A Claude query is far less likely to lead to a congressional hearing or a call from the foreign ministry than a well-written and nuanced report or op-ed.
insights.locator: we will miss out on the credentialing effect

insights.claim: Withholding work from models is fundamentally a bet that human researchers can keep producing better and fresher insights than exceptionally powerful models through research, dialogue, and fieldwork.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Clean decision framework for any content owner weighing licensing versus withholding: it reduces to a confidence bet on your own rate of improvement versus the models'.
insights.quote: You can’t put our intellectual caviar in your AI soup, but you can come to us and eat it on its own.
insights.locator: In some sense, we will need to decide

insights.claim: Philanthropic funders need demonstrable attributable impact, and if research becomes mostly grist for model mills that attribution vanishes — pushing organizations toward direct consultation and bespoke research products.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Funding-model pressure, not ideology, is the mechanism that could convert public think tanks into paid advisory shops — watch for bespoke research and consultation revenue lines.
insights.quote: Driving direct consultation with our experts and engagement with bespoke research products might become a more important part of how we demonstrate our ongoing impact on public decisionmaking.
insights.locator: Whatever our view on the wisdom of such a shift

insights.claim: Because AI makes dataset construction cost-efficient, proprietary data — rather than the packaging and distribution of analysis — becomes the potential comparative advantage for research institutions.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Value in research shifts from output layer to input layer; proprietary data assets are the thing to build and to value.
insights.quote: Those data—more than the packaging and distribution of them—have the potential to be a comparative advantage.
insights.locator: If we do evolve into a collection of scholars

insights.claim: Research organizations systematically waste privately gathered intelligence — conversations with German defense manufacturers, Ukrainian frontline soldiers, closed-door critical minerals convenings — because it is used only by the researcher who collected it.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Internal AI knowledge management is a concrete, near-term efficiency unlock in any organization whose main asset is undocumented human conversation.
insights.quote: The content collected in our research process is inefficiently used—usually only by the researcher or researchers who collected it
insights.locator: AI also expands the possibilities for internal knowledge management

insights.claim: Shifting toward private research would turn a public-good institution into something closer to a private intelligence organization dedicated to the public good, changing its identity as much as its operations.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Institutional identity, not just economics, is the binding constraint on this pivot — which is why it will be slow and contested.
insights.quote: If we were to shift in some meaningful ways to being something more like a private intelligence organization that is dedicated to the public good
insights.locator: The public nature of our work

insights.claim: Professionals across journalism, law, academia, public service, and finance share a 'collective flinch' — a consistent expectation of a coming disruptive tipping point even where optimism about outcomes differs.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: A read on white-collar sentiment: anticipatory paralysis is widespread, which itself slows adaptation and creates advantage for early movers.
insights.quote: Most professionals I know—whatever their field—appear to me today to be in a kind of collective flinch, as if anticipating a painful blow.
insights.locator: Most professionals I know

insights.claim: Public AI discourse has matured from 'frothy' punditry three years ago — confident, contradictory predictions with few real experts — into humbler, better-substantiated debate rooted in an identifiable epistemic community.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Sentiment maturity marker: the hype-cycle punditry phase has passed, which typically precedes more durable, less narrative-driven capital allocation.
insights.quote: Three years ago, I often described the public discourse around AI as “frothy.”
insights.locator: Three years ago, I often described

insights.claim: Holding an explicit 'vision subject to revision' beats waiting for AI to happen to you, both for adaptation odds and for organizational morale.
insights.speaker: Dan Baer

insights.quote: Waiting for AI to happen to us can’t be the most effective way to maintain our emotional well-being
insights.locator: But I believe that having some sort of vision

insights.claim: Organizations will resist changing the comfortable and familiar parts of their work while welcoming AI for nuisances, so the right posture is to be 'clever conservatives or selective revolutionaries.'
insights.speaker: Dan Baer
insights.so_what: Predicts the specific shape of institutional AI resistance: adoption where it is painless, resistance where it touches identity — useful for handicapping incumbent transformation.

insights.claim: If AI's transformation is comparable to past technological and political-economy shifts, challenges to peace are likely to increase rather than decrease.
